# SwarmOps

> A git replacement for swarms of coding agents: many agents commit into one embedded store at once, every command answers in JSON, and the work moves back to git. It is written in Rust, MIT licensed and pre-1.0, and runs on Linux today, with macOS and Windows next.

SwarmOps is designed for 10 to 50 Claude Code or LangGraph processes on one host, committing to one repository at once. It is one program with no external database and no daemon. Object writes take no lock, metadata writes queue in the kernel for one lock, and refs move only by compare-and-swap; on one host, 32 processes have committed 1,000 times each through the binary without one `E_BUSY`. `land` merges an agent's change three-way onto `main` without a checkout, merges again when `main` moves, and reports a conflict as `E_CONFLICT` with a JSON report. Commands print a JSON envelope on stdout; only help and version text print plain text, and `swarmops mcp` speaks MCP there instead. A failure carries a stable `E_*` code, a fixed exit code, whether retrying can help, machine-readable `details` and a `hint`, often the next command to run. `swarmops mcp` serves the operations to MCP clients such as Claude Code as 18 tools. `git import` and `git export` are commands, not MCP tools: they bring a history in from git and send landed work back, so that today's deployment pipelines keep running.

Limits: SwarmOps is not meant as a general-purpose git replacement, and git parity is not a v1 goal. It has no user hooks, signing, submodules or LFS, and its refs are `main` and `release/<name>` only. Until workspaces arrive (M5), an agent cannot build or test a change on disk before it lands it. It runs on Linux today (built and tested on x86_64, with the store on a native Linux filesystem), with macOS and Windows next (M12). It has no network code: every operation runs against the host's own store, and between hosts, work moves through a git remote, one writing host at a time. Writers take turns at one lock, so its throughput is behind agents in git worktrees by design; no git baseline has been measured, and landing has not been measured under a swarm's load. It is pre-1.0: a minor version may break a public surface other than the hash contract, and there is no migration tool for store formats before 1.0.

## What SwarmOps is

- [SwarmOps website](https://swarmops.cc/): The landing page: why a swarm of agents is not a team of people, how the store works, how SwarmOps compares with git dimension by dimension, a quick start, the MCP tools and the roadmap.
- [SwarmOps on GitHub](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps): The source code, the README and the issue tracker.

## Guides

- [Parallel coding agents on one repository](https://swarmops.cc/guides/parallel-agents): How many coding agents commit to one repository with SwarmOps: one store, refs moved by compare-and-swap, three-way landing, and where git worktrees still lead.
- [Use SwarmOps from Claude Code over MCP](https://swarmops.cc/guides/claude-code): Register `swarmops mcp` with Claude Code, give each agent process its own identity, and follow the two rules agents need: full ids for compare-and-swap, small results.
- [Keep git: import, land and export](https://swarmops.cc/guides/git-round-trip): Bring a git repository into a SwarmOps store, let agents land their work, and export it back to git so CI and deployment keep running.

## Explainers

- [The SwarmOps store, as a machine](https://swarmops.cc/explainers/store): Fig. 1, an interactive drawing of the store: writers wait for one lock, which the kernel hands to one of them at a time, in no strict order, and each commit becomes one CRC-framed frame of the journal; objects need no lock.

## README and documentation on GitHub

- [README](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/README.md): Why SwarmOps, how it compares with git, how it works, quick start, MCP, every command and exit code, and the roadmap.
- [SwarmOps architecture](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/docs/architecture.md): The design in English: crates, data model, the store on disk, the write and read paths, durability, concurrency, the contract.
- [Operating SwarmOps](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/docs/operations.md): Running SwarmOps: install, a store, agents through MCP, the daily loop between the store and git, checks, backup and restore, upgrades, limits and what to monitor.
- [Known limitations](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/docs/known-limitations.md): What is still open, and which milestone takes each item.
- [Versioning and stability](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/docs/policies/versioning-and-stability.md): What stays compatible, and how a breaking change is made.
- [Toolchain, MSRV and platforms](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/docs/policies/msrv-and-platforms.md): The Rust version and the platforms SwarmOps supports.
- [Changelog](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/CHANGELOG.md): What has changed, with every breaking change called out under its version.
- [Contributing to SwarmOps](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/CONTRIBUTING.md): How changes are made and the tests' rules.
- [Security policy](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/SECURITY.md): How to report a vulnerability privately, and what counts as one.
- [License](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/LICENSE): The MIT License.

## Optional

- [Performance ledger](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/docs/perf.md): Every measurement, and the decisions taken on them.
- [Benchmark harness](https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/blob/stable/bench/compare/README.md): The harness that measures the native metadata store against embedded databases.
